column5: creation by command
column6: The commentary grounds praise in the Creator's work rather than a remote epithet; Genesis has light come to be at God's spoken command, giving a concrete scriptural scene of creation by word.

column5: formed earthling and breath
column6: The commentary reads 87:2 as including the listener's body and later discusses form before spirit; Genesis depicts YHWH forming the human from soil and breathing life into him.

column5: completed creation called very good
column6: The commentary hears خلق and سوى as making and completing a fitting whole; after the six days God sees all that he made as very good, an explicit judgment on completed form.

column5: praise the Name because he commanded creation
column6: The commentary attaches praise of the Lord's Name to the deeds that identify him; this praise summons creation to praise that Name because he commanded and they came to be.

column5: creation in a worship litany
column6: The commentary treats glorifying the Name as grounded in works; Nehemiah's prayer names the maker of heavens, earth and sea, says he gives life to all, and ends with heaven's host worshiping.

column5: measures of waters, sky and mountains
column6: The commentary holds together creation, measured proportion and the ordered heavens; Isaiah asks who measured the waters, spanned the heavens and weighed the mountains, making cosmic order the Creator's work.

column5: earth measured and line set
column6: The commentary's artisan measures before cutting, while the Creator needs no model; Job's question about who set earth's measures and stretched its line makes cosmic measurement a divine act.

column5: earth formed to be inhabited
column6: The commentary says the Most High is known inside his work, not moved beyond the sky; Isaiah says the maker formed the earth to be inhabited rather than leaving it empty.

column5: blessing the Lord in view of his works
column6: The commentary's opening links praise of the Name to the deeds that reveal the Lord; this psalm blesses YHWH and immediately describes his majestic ordering of light and heavens.

column5: grass made for people and animals
column6: The commentary connects creation's ordering with pasture as provision for people and livestock; the psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human use.

column5: withdrawn breath and returning dust
column6: The commentary holds completed form beside aging and decay; the psalm says creatures die and return to dust when God hides his face and takes away their breath.

column5: breath creates and renews the earth
column6: The commentary connects bodily formation, breath and the later reversal of creation; this verse says God sends his spirit, creatures are created, and the face of the ground is renewed.

column5: praise for a wonderfully made body
column6: The commentary says the hearer can find the Creator's work in their own body; the psalmist praises God because he is wondrously formed, joining bodily making directly to praise.

column5: unformed substance and numbered days
column6: The commentary's womb discussion treats the body as shaped before its life unfolds; the psalmist says God's eyes saw his unformed substance and his days were written before they came.

column5: God's thoughts beyond counting
column6: The commentary moves from the body as evidence of its Maker to the Maker's knowledge; in the same psalm, God's thoughts are too many to count, extending the creation scene into divine knowledge.

column5: hands fashioned and shaped the speaker
column6: The commentary compares creation to measured craft while denying the Creator's dependence on a pattern; Job addresses God as the one whose hands fashioned and shaped him.

column5: embryonic shaping like milk and curd
column6: The commentary develops the body collected and ordered in the womb; Job depicts conception through the concrete sequence of pouring him out like milk and curdling him like cheese.

column5: skin, flesh, bones and sinews
column6: The commentary's body image is one of parts brought into proportion; Job lists skin, flesh, bones and sinews as God's work in forming him.

column5: formed in the womb and appointed to a task
column6: The commentary links measured making with an apt direction; Jeremiah says God knew, set apart and appointed him before birth, joining prenatal formation to a particular vocation.

column5: Creator forms the human spirit within
column6: The commentary extends proportioning from the body to inward life; Zechariah names the one who forms the human spirit within as the maker of heavens and earth.

column5: one Maker forms master and servant in the womb
column6: The commentary locates the Creator's trace in the listener's body; Job says the same maker formed both him and his servant in the womb, giving shared creation an explicit social consequence.

column5: unseen formation of bones in the womb
column6: The commentary stresses that bodily formation exceeds human observation; Qoheleth compares the unknown development of bones in a pregnant woman's womb with God's work.

column5: sinews, flesh, skin before breath
column6: The commentary discusses a formed body awaiting the breath of life; Ezekiel's dry-bones vision orders sinews, flesh and skin before breath, making restoration follow a bodily sequence.

column5: breath makes the assembled bodies live
column6: The commentary joins completed form to life-giving breath; in Ezekiel's vision the bodies stand alive only after breath enters them.

column5: formed senses imply the Maker hears and sees
column6: The commentary uses the body as a trace of the Creator's work; the psalm asks whether the one who planted the ear cannot hear and formed the eye cannot see, drawing divine knowledge from bodily design.

column5: God fashions every heart
column6: The commentary develops proportioning beyond visible form to inward character; this verse says God fashions the hearts of all and attends to their deeds.

column5: the maker who made and established Israel
column6: The commentary identifies the Lord by what he does; Moses asks whether YHWH is Israel's father and maker, the one who made and established them, making creation grounds for covenant loyalty.

column5: God rides the clouds as his chariot
column6: The commentary contrasts the Most High with a being transported beyond the sky; the psalm pictures YHWH riding the clouds, a concrete image for comparison whose own setting celebrates his power over creation.

column5: God rides the heavens to aid Israel
column6: The commentary says the Most High is known by works rather than carried beyond the sky; Moses' blessing pictures Israel's God riding the heavens to help them, a contrasting sky image framed as protective nearness.

column5: prepare a straight way for YHWH
column6: The commentary joins making complete to the straight road of guidance; Isaiah calls for a highway in the wilderness for God, turning a straightened path into preparation for his arrival.

column5: valleys raised and rough ground leveled
column6: The commentary gives سوى both completion and straightening, then links it to a road; Isaiah's next verse levels valleys and mountains and makes rough country a plain.

column5: just balances belong to YHWH
column6: The commentary defines the سوى family through balance between things and protection from excess or deficiency; Proverbs applies that measure to fair weights and says the scales belong to YHWH.

column5: YHWH sets the speaker's allotted portion
column6: The commentary explicitly labels an Arabic branch of خ ل ق as a measured share; the psalm says the lines fell to the speaker in pleasant places and YHWH holds his lot, a concrete allotment image without importing it as the ayah's main sense.

column5: polished arrow hidden until its mission
column6: The commentary describes an arrow measured, smoothed and aimed as the next ayah's guidance image; Isaiah's servant says God made him a polished arrow and hid him in a quiver until his word was needed.

column5: earth wears out like a garment
column6: The commentary develops smoothness as the worn nap of a garment and the leveling of a ruined trace; Isaiah says earth wears out like clothing, while the heavens vanish like smoke.

column5: grass withers under the Lord's breath
column6: The commentary follows pasture from emergence to darkened refuse; Isaiah says grass withers when YHWH's breath blows on it, making the created pasture's transience explicit.

column5: water given from split rock
column6: The commentary's rock image is a hollow that catches and holds rainwater; the psalm recalls God splitting rocks in the wilderness and giving drink from the depths, a related but reversed movement of water from rock.

column5: streams from the cliff
column6: The commentary describes a hollow in stone retaining water that would otherwise run off; this verse says God brought streams from the rock and made waters flow down like rivers.

column5: water comes out of the struck rock
column6: The commentary's rock-and-water image makes stone a place where water is retained; at Horeb God tells Moses to strike the rock, from which water comes for the people.

column5: blessing after God guides a journey
column6: The commentary joins travel, a mount and remembering the Lord's favor; Abraham's servant blesses YHWH after recognizing that God led him on the way to his master's kin.

column5: horses contrasted with invoking God's Name
column6: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord on a rider's back; the psalm contrasts those who trust chariots and horses with those who invoke YHWH's Name.

column5: idols are made by human hands
column6: The commentary contrasts the Creator's unmodeled work with human fabrication and false worship; this psalm names silver-and-gold idols as human handiwork.

column5: idols have mouths but cannot speak
column6: The commentary rejects the creature's fabricated claim as a counterfeit of the Creator; the psalm's handmade images have mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see.

column5: makers become like their idols
column6: The commentary says a lie made by a creature imitates the Creator's act but has no reality; the psalm says idol-makers and trusters become like the speechless images they fashion.

column5: measured carving made into a human likeness
column6: The commentary contrasts a human artisan who measures and cuts with the Creator who needs no prior model; Isaiah describes the woodworker measuring and carving an image in human form.

column5: one piece of wood becomes fuel and an idol
column6: The commentary exposes created objects as poor substitutes for their Maker; Isaiah says the same wood supplies fire and is also made into a god for worship.

column5: the remnant of wood is called a god
column6: The commentary's created-versus-counterfeit contrast turns on the maker's false claim; Isaiah's image-maker bows to the leftover wood and asks it to save him.

column5: Creator stretches the heavens alone
column6: The commentary says the Lord is known by works and needs no model or partner; Isaiah names YHWH as maker of all things who stretches the heavens alone.

column5: earth established by wisdom and understanding
column6: The commentary presents creation as measured and completed work; Jeremiah says God made earth by power and established the world by wisdom and understanding.

column5: idol-makers' images are false and breathless
column6: The commentary contrasts true creation with fabricated claims; Jeremiah says the images made by craftsmen are a lie and have no breath.

column5: Maker of all versus worthless idols
column6: The commentary grounds praise in the one who truly creates; Jeremiah contrasts the portion of Jacob, who made all things, with idols that are not like him.

column5: God bears Israel from the womb
column6: The commentary's riding image places a human on an animal; Isaiah reverses the carrying relation by portraying God as the one who has carried Israel from birth.

column5: God carries Israel through old age
column6: The commentary connects formed bodies with later aging and wear; Isaiah promises that the God who carried Israel from the womb will carry them even into old age.

column5: the humble king comes riding a donkey
column6: The commentary describes a rider settling on an animal and remembering the Lord; Zechariah's king arrives humbly on a donkey, a royal riding scene whose Gospel reception adds public praise.

column5: Jesus enters as king on a donkey
column6: Matthew applies Zechariah's donkey-riding king to Jesus; beside the commentary's rider who praises the Creator of the mount, the difference is that this crowd welcomes the rider as king.

column5: crowd blesses the one who comes in the Lord's Name
column6: The commentary has the mounted worshiper say praise to the Creator who subjected the animal; Matthew's crowd blesses the arriving king in the Lord's Name, shifting the praised figure while retaining the liturgical formula.

column5: create a clean heart and renew the spirit
column6: The commentary extends proportioning from the body to the soul's moral direction; this prayer asks God to create a clean heart and renew a steadfast spirit, making inner ordering a new creation.

column5: neither add to nor subtract from the command
column6: The commentary mentions a separate Arabic form for omitting a letter and places it beside the promise of recitation without forgetting; Moses likewise forbids adding to or subtracting from God's command.

column5: the king cuts and burns the scroll
column6: The commentary's secondary root sense is dropping a letter from scripture; Jeremiah depicts Jehoiakim cutting the divine scroll with a knife and burning it, a concrete opposite to preserving recitation.

column5: valleys filled and crooked roads straightened
column6: Luke applies Isaiah's leveling image to preparation for God's salvation; it gives the commentary's link between completed form and a straight path an explicit prophetic and ethical setting.

column5: all flesh sees God's salvation
column6: The commentary says the Creator's work is witnessed in the hearer's body; Luke's next line says all flesh will see God's salvation, widening the prepared road to a universal audience.

column5: rain makes the earth bud and seed grow
column6: The commentary connects ordered creation with water, pasture and provision; Isaiah says rain waters the earth, makes it bud and supplies seed and bread, giving a specific scriptural path from creation to food.

column5: birds fed without sowing or harvest
column6: The commentary treats created life as provision for people and animals; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor reap yet are fed by the Father, a specific ethical inference from creation's ordering.

column5: grain grows through stages to full ear
column6: The commentary describes a shoot strengthening, thickening and standing on its stalk; Mark's seed parable likewise names the ordered sequence of blade, ear and full grain.

column5: Creator is not contained in human temples
column6: The commentary says the Most High is not carried beyond the sky and is known by his works; Paul says the Maker of the world does not dwell in temples built by human hands.

column5: God gives life and breath rather than receiving service
column6: The commentary contrasts the Creator with creatures and formed objects; Paul says God is not served by human hands but gives all people life and breath.

column5: nations receive appointed times and boundaries
column6: The commentary's creation includes measured portions and subsequent guidance; Paul says God made every nation and fixed its times and boundaries, then connects those limits to seeking God.

column5: humans are meant to seek God who is near
column6: The commentary links a made and proportioned creature to guidance; Paul says the nations' appointed setting is so they might seek God, who is not far from each person.

column5: divinity is not gold, stone or human craft
column6: The commentary contrasts the Creator with images that creatures fabricate; Paul says divine nature cannot be like gold, silver or stone shaped by human art and imagination.

column5: all things came to be through the Word
column6: The commentary stresses that the Creator needs no prior mold; John says all things came to be through the Word and not one created thing came to be apart from him.

column5: all things created through and for Christ
column6: The commentary's objectless verb is said to encompass all creation; Colossians names visible and invisible things and every rank as created through and for Christ.

column5: worship because God created all things
column6: The commentary grounds the command to glorify the Name in God's creative deeds; Revelation's heavenly worship says all things exist because God willed and created them.

column5: visible things made from what is not visible
column6: The commentary says خ ل ق can cover originating without a model as well as bringing forth from something; Hebrews says the visible order was not made from visible things, making the unseen-origin reading explicit.

column5: God made heaven and earth from what did not exist
column6: The commentary preserves creation both without a prior mold and from something else; the mother in 2 Maccabees explicitly tells her son that God made heaven and earth not from existing things.

column5: all things ordered by measure, number and weight
column6: The commentary's measuring artisan image develops creation as proportion rather than decoration; Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number and weight.

column5: paired works and nothing incomplete
column6: The commentary defines سوى as balance between things and protection from excess or deficiency; Ben Sira says all things are in pairs and God has made nothing incomplete.

column5: God made all things by his word
column6: The commentary joins the Creator's work to a command that needs no tool or mold; Solomon's prayer names God as the one who made all things by his word.

column5: human formed by wisdom
column6: The commentary's bodily formation becomes a human made in fitting relation to the world; this prayer says God formed humanity by wisdom.

column5: all humans from earth, then distinguished
column6: The commentary moves from common creation to each creature's measured share; Ben Sira says all humans come from earth and then describes the Most High distinguishing their ways.

column5: humanity as clay in the Maker's hand
column6: The commentary's artisan measures material before shaping it; Ben Sira directly compares the human being in the Maker's hand to clay in the potter's hand.

column5: living soul rendered speaking spirit
column6: The commentary extends bodily making toward inner capacities and the danger of false speech; Onkelos renders the human's resulting life as a speaking spirit, making rational speech part of the creation scene.

column5: one first human, many distinct faces
column6: The commentary's objectless creation includes every hearer's body; the Mishnah says one human was created first, yet no two people resemble each other, grounding shared origin and individual form in human dignity.

column5: God's spirit equips a human artisan
column6: The commentary compares measured craft to divine creation without a model; Exodus says Bezalel is filled with God's spirit, wisdom and skill for craftsmanship, making human making a capacity received from the Creator.

column5: potter remakes a spoiled vessel
column6: The commentary's craft image distinguishes a maker's measured work from later wear and failure; Jeremiah shows a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand being remade into another form.

column5: we are clay and God our potter
column6: The commentary uses human craft to illuminate divine forming; Isaiah turns the same relation into confession and plea, calling Israel clay and YHWH its potter.

column5: the formed thing questions its maker
column6: The commentary distinguishes the Creator's measured work from a creature's false judgment; Paul asks whether what is formed can say to its molder, Why did you make me this way?

column5: God places each member in the body as he wills
column6: The commentary describes سوى as parts brought into relation without excess or lack; Paul says God arranged each body member in its place, giving that proportioning a communal consequence.

column5: God composes the body and honors weaker parts
column6: The commentary says a sound whole is made by relation among its parts; Paul says God composed the body and gave greater honor to the part that lacked it, turning proportion into care for the weak.

column5: created for good works prepared beforehand
column6: The commentary connects measured making to guidance along a path; Paul calls believers God's workmanship, created in Christ for good works God prepared for them to walk in.

column5: creation makes God's power perceptible
column6: The commentary says the Creator is known in the works rather than beyond the sky; Paul says God's invisible power is perceived through what has been made.

column5: Creator's glory exchanged for images
column6: The commentary opposes the one who creates to images made by human hands; Paul describes people exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal humans and animals.

column5: creature worship replaces Creator worship
column6: The commentary says a fabricated lie imitates the Creator's act and misdirects worship; Paul says people exchanged truth for a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator.

column5: failure to know God from created works
column6: The commentary says the Lord is identified by what he has made; Wisdom criticizes people who failed to recognize the artisan from the beauty of his works.

column5: handmade images called worthless gods
column6: The commentary contrasts real creation with false objects of worship; Wisdom calls the nations' handmade idols worthless gods and condemns their makers' craft.

column5: the Lord laid earth's foundation
column6: The commentary includes the ordered sky and earth in the Creator's objectless work; Hebrews applies the psalm's creation words to the Son, who laid earth's foundation and made the heavens.

column5: he heavens wear out like clothing
column6: The commentary develops smoothness as wear that erases the nap of a garment; Hebrews says the heavens will perish and wear out like clothing.

column5: creation freed from decay
column6: The commentary connects completed creation with the later wearing-down of bodies and land; Paul says creation itself will be freed from its slavery to decay.

column5: Jesus breathes the Spirit onto the disciples
column6: The commentary connects formed body and breath; after the resurrection Jesus breathes on the disciples and gives the Holy Spirit, reusing the creation gesture for a renewed community.

column5: first Adam lives, last Adam gives life
column6: The commentary's formation-and-breath sequence is applied to human origin and resurrection; Paul quotes the first Adam as a living being and calls Christ the life-giving Spirit, giving the creation scene an eschatological reading.

column5: Jesus grows in wisdom and stature
column6: The commentary says a person may reach completion of youth and then receive knowledge; Luke describes Jesus increasing in wisdom and stature, a concrete Christian account of growth toward maturity.

column5: Jesus forms clay sparrows on the Sabbath
column6: The commentary compares Jesus shaping a clay bird, breathing into it and acting by God's permission; this infancy narrative has the child Jesus make twelve clay sparrows on the Sabbath and clap them alive, relocating the scene to childhood and omitting the Qur'anic repeated permission formula.

column5: heavens stretched like a tent
column6: The commentary says the Most High is known in his works rather than displaced beyond the sky; the psalm's next verse describes God stretching out the heavens, making the sky itself an act of his ordering.

column5: humanity created male and female
column6: The commentary's surrounding creation citations include the making of pairs; Genesis states that God created humanity in his image as male and female, a specific paired form within the creation account.

column5: Jesus invokes creation of male and female
column6: The commentary notes the created pairs in its wider account; Jesus cites the Creator making male and female and uses their joining to explain marriage, giving that creation formula a relational interpretation.

column5: God remembers humans are dust
column6: The commentary connects bodily form with the vulnerability of aging; the psalm says God knows our frame and remembers that we are dust, linking care to the material from which humans were made.

column5: perishable body raised imperishable
column6: The commentary's wear and leveling imagery reaches bodily death and renewed creation; Paul says the body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, distinguishing the formed body from its resurrection condition.

column5: natural body raised as spiritual body
column6: The commentary connects bodily form with breath and resurrection; Paul distinguishes the natural body from the spiritual body, giving the Adamic formation image an eschatological continuation.

column5: bones interpreted as the restored house of Israel
column6: The commentary's womb-and-breath sequence can sound solely bodily; Ezekiel explicitly interprets the assembled bones as all Israel restored to its land, giving the same image a national rather than anatomical referent.

column5: Moses' strength remains at 120
column6: The commentary connects ordered bodily life with aging's reversal; Deuteronomy presents Moses at 120 with undimmed eye and undiminished vigor, a specific counterexample to simple physical decline.

column5: world formed from formless matter
column6: The commentary allows both creation without an exemplar and making one thing from another; Wisdom describes God's hand forming the world from formless matter, a distinct ancient Jewish account of the latter possibility.

column5: one work confirms the good of another
column6: The commentary says a proportioned thing is fitted in relation to other things; Ben Sira adds that one work confirms another's good and that this ordered whole displays divine glory.

column5: human appointed to govern creation
column6: The commentary links making to the apt direction that follows; Solomon asks for wisdom to govern the world and judge rightly, making the human creature's purpose explicit.

column5: created humans retain choice
column6: The commentary pairs creation with guidance without describing humans as inert; Ben Sira says God created humans and left them in the hand of their own counsel, making moral agency explicit.

column5: life and death set before human choice
column6: The commentary develops measured creation and a way to be followed; Ben Sira says fire and water are set before the hearer to choose, clarifying that guidance still addresses an agent.

column5: life or death according to the choice
column6: The commentary's creation-and-guidance sequence can be read alongside human response; Ben Sira says life and death are before each person and what they choose is given to them.

column5: opposite works set against one another
column6: The commentary describes balance and its contrary, flattening and decay; Ben Sira says the works of the Most High stand in pairs, one opposite the other.

column5: human beloved as created in God's image
column6: The commentary asks the hearer to find the Lord's work in their own body; Akiva's saying makes being created in God's image the reason humanity is beloved.

column5: creation debated by Truth, Peace and Righteousness
column6: The commentary contrasts the true Creator with lies fabricated by creatures; the midrash places Truth, Peace and Righteousness in debate over humanity's creation, then depicts Truth cast to earth, complicating the ethical meaning of making humans.

column5: fetus taught Torah before birth
column6: The commentary presents the womb as a place where a body is formed for later direction; this rabbinic image says a fetus is taught Torah before birth and forgets it on entering the world, adding a tradition of prenatal moral capacity.

column5: two spirits and two human paths
column6: The commentary links inner formation to the later distinction between uprightness and deviation; the Community Rule describes humanity as walking in two spirits, truth and injustice, giving a specific sectarian account of moral direction.

column5: Israel is clay in the potter's hand
column6: The commentary portrays creation as exacting work without making it a fixed mold; Jeremiah applies potter and clay to Israel, where the image concerns a people God may reshape in response to their conduct.

column5: one potter makes vessels for different uses
column6: The commentary says measured creation makes things fit their purpose; Paul asks whether a potter may use the same clay for different vessels, adding a question of divine choice and human limits.

column5: members care equally for one another
column6: The commentary's balance is not mere leveling but relational fitness; Paul explains that the body is arranged so there is no division and members care for one another.

column5: joined body grows as each part works
column6: The commentary's body image treats completion as a relation among parts; Ephesians describes the whole body joined and held together as each part works, producing growth.

column5: humans made in God's likeness
column6: The commentary's praise of the Creator rejects false speech and false worship; James says the same tongue blesses God and curses human beings made in God's likeness, making creation a test of speech.

column5: greatness of works points to their Maker
column6: The commentary makes the Creator's works the basis of praise; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of created things let observers infer their Maker.

column5: the potter shapes vessels from the same clay
column6: The commentary's artisan scene measures material into a useful form; Wisdom describes a potter shaping the same clay into vessels for different uses, adding a Jewish reflection on craft and purpose.

column5: the maker is mortal but the image has no breath
column6: The commentary contrasts the living Creator with fabricated forms; Wisdom says the maker is mortal and the handmade image has no breath, sharpening the difference between life-giving creation and craft.

column5: he worn creation is changed while God remains
column6: The commentary holds ordered creation beside its eventual leveling and decay; Hebrews says the heavens will be rolled up like a cloak and changed while the Lord remains the same.

column5: creation groans in labor pains
column6: The commentary traces formation through bodily development and later decay; Paul pictures the whole creation groaning together in labor pains, making decay part of a hoped-for new birth.

column5: Moses goes out when grown
column6: The commentary connects the completion of youth to Moses' later receiving wisdom and judgment; Exodus marks the point when Moses has grown up before he acts among his people.

column5: humanity grows gradually toward perfection
column6: The commentary extends سوى from a complete body to the completion of youth; Irenaeus reads human beings as created immature and brought gradually to perfection, making development a feature of the Creator's pedagogy.

column5: tree by water bears fruit and does not wither
column6: The commentary contrasts water's useful remainder with foam that washes away; Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a tree by streams whose fruit endures, adding an ethical reading of what remains fruitful.

column5: chaff blown away by the wind
column6: The commentary's flood image distinguishes useful matter from passing foam; Psalm 1 contrasts the enduring tree with wicked people as chaff driven away, applying the separation to conduct.

column5: serpent contradicts the Creator's warning
column6: The commentary describes fabrication as a creature's internally measured falsehood set against the Creator's true word; the serpent tells the humans they will not die, directly contradicting God's instruction.

column5: human life like grass and a field flower
column6: The commentary follows pasture from emergence to withering refuse; this psalm compares human days to grass and the flower of the field, applying the same transience to a life God remembers.

column5: wind passes and the flower is gone
column6: The commentary treats smoothness from wear as a sign of ending; the psalm says the wind passes over the flower and its place knows it no more, a concrete image of disappearance.

column5: dust returns to earth and spirit to God
column6: The commentary links formed bodies with aging and death; Qoheleth closes the aging sequence by saying dust returns to earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

column5: grass fades but God's word stands
column6: The commentary juxtaposes fading pasture with the promise that recitation will be preserved; Isaiah says grass withers and flowers fade while God's word stands forever.

column5: God makes the path straight
column6: The commentary joins proportioning to guidance along a straight road; Proverbs says to acknowledge God in every way and he will make the paths straight.

column5: teach the speaker God's paths
column6: The commentary pairs a made creature with the Creator's guidance; the psalm asks YHWH to lead and teach the speaker in his paths, making direction an explicit response to dependence.

column5: lead in truth and teach
column6: The commentary connects being made fit with being guided; the psalm asks God to lead the speaker in truth and teach him, a prayer for a path rather than a claim about bodily form.

column5: human crowned and given rule over creation
column6: The commentary says creation's unnamed object includes the hearer; this psalm places humanity within the created order as crowned with glory and given responsibility over God's works.

column5: intelligible paradigm behind the visible world
column6: The commentary presents the Creator as measuring without consulting a prior mold; Philo reads Genesis through an intelligible paradigm for the cosmos, giving a Jewish interpretation that makes the model question explicit.

column5: Hebrew שוה and Arabic سوى
column6: The source commentary explicitly labels the سوى root as straightness and balance; Hebrew שוה here means making equal in a challenge about God's incomparability, a likely cognate connection whose lexeme does not by itself establish the Qur'anic verb's meaning.

column5: Hebrew חלק and the source's smoothness branch
column6: The source commentary explicitly labels خ ل ق B008 as smoothness; Hebrew חלק describes Jacob's smooth skin here, a possible cognate with Arabic خ ل ق in that secondary branch, though the etymology is uncertain and does not define 87:2.

column5: created and formed Israel, called by name
column6: The commentary says the Lord is identified by deeds rather than a remote epithet; Isaiah names YHWH as the one who created and formed Jacob, redeemed him and called him by name.

column5: created and formed for God's glory
column6: The commentary ties glorifying the Lord's Name to the works that identify him; Isaiah says the people called by God's name were created and formed for his glory.

column5: formed Israel from the womb
column6: The commentary develops bodily formation in the womb as a secondary sense alongside creation; Isaiah names YHWH as the one who made and formed Jacob from the womb and will help him.

column5: Hebrew שוה, leveling a field before sowing
column6: The source commentary explicitly labels سوى with straightening and balance; Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה for leveling a field's surface before seed is sown, a close cognate use in an agricultural setting that does not determine the Qur'anic verb's full sense.

column5: hands make and fashion, then grant understanding
column6: The commentary joins being made to the guidance that follows; the psalmist says God's hands made and fashioned him, then asks for understanding to learn God's commands.

column5: Spirit leads the speaker on level ground
column6: The commentary connects proportioning, guidance and the straight path; the psalm asks God to teach his will and let his good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground.

column5: life and breath of every creature in God's hand
column6: The commentary treats each body as evidence of its Maker and develops breath as the completion of form; Job says the life of every creature and breath of humankind are in God's hand.

column5: God's Spirit makes and breath gives life
column6: The commentary connects bodily formation to life-giving breath; Job says the Spirit of God made him and the breath of the Almighty gives him life.

column5: life, care and steadfast love preserve the spirit
column6: The commentary says the formed body bears the trace of the Lord's work; Job adds that the same God who formed him granted life and care that preserved his spirit.

column5: created humans receive a task and blessing
column6: The commentary links creation to the suitable direction that follows; after creating male and female, Genesis blesses them and gives them a role toward the other creatures.

column5: idols are nothing, YHWH made the heavens
column6: The commentary contrasts the Creator with things fabricated for worship; the psalm calls the nations' gods idols and says YHWH made the heavens.

column5: worship before YHWH the Maker
column6: The commentary ties glorification to the Creator's acts; the psalm calls the congregation to bow before YHWH because he is their Maker.

column5: blessing for the body's openings and functions
column6: The commentary asks the hearer to recognize the Creator in the body's fitted parts; this rabbinic blessing thanks God for forming the human body with its openings and cavities, whose obstruction would prevent life.

column5: the Maker forms, inspires soul and breathes life
column6: The commentary contrasts the living Creator with lifeless images made by artisans; Wisdom says the idol-maker failed to know the one who formed him, inspired an active soul and breathed a living spirit into him.

column5: Solomon molded in the womb like every human
column6: The commentary develops bodily formation before birth and the common human process; Solomon says he too was molded in flesh in his mother's womb and received breath like all people.

column5: humans made in God's image
column6: The commentary reads creation as including the listener's own body; Ben Sira says God endowed humans with strength and made them in his image.

column5: eyes, ears and a thinking heart
column6: The commentary extends proportioned creation to inward and sensory capacities; Ben Sira says God gave humans discernment, eyes, ears and a heart for thinking.

column5: knowledge of good and evil
column6: The commentary links making with subsequent moral direction; Ben Sira says God filled humanity with knowledge and understanding and showed them good and evil.

column5: rewritten scroll includes all former words and more
column6: The commentary sets the secondary image of omitting a letter beside the promise of preserved recitation; after the king burns the scroll, Jeremiah dictates it again with all its former words and many more.

column5: water wears stone and washes soil away
column6: The commentary describes smoothness as wear that flattens a surface; Job says waters wear stones and torrents wash away the soil, giving a direct image of erosion.

column5: Tyre's walls reduced to bare rock
column6: The commentary connects the smooth rock with a settlement leveled to the ground; Ezekiel's oracle says Tyre's walls and towers will be broken, its dust scraped away and the site left like bare rock.

column5: Zion plowed like a field and Jerusalem made ruins
column6: The commentary links سوى's leveling sense to the end of a created settlement; Micah warns that Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of ruins because of its rulers' injustice.

column5: woman from man, man through woman, all from God
column6: The commentary describes parts as fitted in relation and notes created pairs; Paul recalls the creation relation between man and woman but concludes that all things are from God.

column5: all things hold together in Christ
column6: The commentary's سوى emphasizes that a whole is made complete through relations among its parts; Colossians says all things hold together in Christ, extending that order to the cosmos.

column5: every hair on the disciples' heads is numbered
column6: The commentary says the listener can find the Creator's work in the body; in a teaching about the Father's care, Jesus says even the hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons and food as witness
column6: The commentary follows creation into pasture and provision for people and animals; Paul says God gives rain, fruitful seasons and food, leaving a witness of his goodness.

column5: man and woman are not independent in the Lord
column6: The commentary describes proportion as relation rather than mere leveling; Paul says woman and man are not independent of one another in the Lord, giving paired creation a mutual reading.

column5: outer person decays while inner person renews
column6: The commentary develops the worn garment and the reversal of bodily order with age; Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed day by day.

column5: spirit, soul and body kept complete
column6: The commentary treats fitting form as extending through body and inward life; Paul prays that the whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless, an explicit Christian formula of integrated completeness.

column5: moon and sun assigned their times
column6: The commentary treats the moon's gradual fullness as completion and cites its phases as measured; the psalm says God appointed the moon for seasons and the sun knows its setting.

column5: all works made in wisdom
column6: The commentary presents the created world as measured and complete; the psalm marvels at the many works of YHWH and says they were all made in wisdom.

column5: creatures wait for food from God
column6: The commentary describes pasture and crop as provision for living creatures; the psalm says all creatures look to God for their food in its season.

column5: God opens his hand and satisfies creatures
column6: The commentary says the created order is fitted to sustain people and animals; the psalm says God gives food when he opens his hand and satisfies every living thing.

column5: humanity made for incorruption in God's image
column6: The commentary connects created form with later bodily wearing and death; Wisdom says God made humans for incorruption and in the image of his own eternity, offering a Jewish account in which death is not the intended completion.

column5: creation includes the heavenly host
column6: The commentary says the ayah's objectless creation can encompass all things; Jubilees' creation account includes the heavens and their host, expanding the creation scene beyond the human body.
